$comment: The design system, as one table of numbers with three readers.
THE PROBLEM THIS IS FOR is the one docs/app-parity.md already names for behaviour,
arriving in a place nobody guards: a value written three times drifts. The console's
greeting is 26px, the iOS greeting is 26pt and the Android greeting is 26sp, and there
is nothing about that arrangement that keeps them equal — a designer moves one, two
surfaces disagree, and the only way to find out is to hold two phones next to a laptop.
ONE FILE, THREE READERS: test/design-parity.test.js reads src/web/console/console.css,
apps/ios/Fleetwright/Design.swift and apps/android/.../Design.kt and asserts each one
declares every token below with this value. Change a number here and all three fail
until all three are updated, which is the point.
WHY A TABLE CAN CHECK THIS WHEN IT COULD NOT CHECK THE REASSURANCE RULE. That rule is
behaviour, so the fixture supplies inputs and both apps run against it. A token is not
behaviour — it IS its literal, written in the source — so reading the three files is
the strongest check available and a genuine one. What it cannot see is a token that is
declared and never used; that is what the per-surface tests are for.
THE NAMES MAP BY A RULE, not by a lookup table. A token `bodySmall` in the `type`
scale is `--t-body-small` in CSS and `Design.Text.bodySmall` in Swift and Kotlin:
kebab-case with the scale's prefix on the web, camelCase in the two apps. A capital
starts a new word and so does a digit, so `chart1` is `--chart-1`.

type.unit: px on the web, pt on iOS, sp on Android

tracking.unit: px / pt / sp, negative — headings only

$comment: Dark first, because dark is the default and the one tuned for a dark room.
`ring` and `highlight` are NOT here. They are the same idea on all three surfaces —
separate a card from the page without drawing a border — and three different
mechanisms: a CSS box-shadow with an inset highlight, a SwiftUI overlay stroke, a
Compose border under an elevation shadow. A shared hex for them would be a number
that agrees while the surfaces do not.
